## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Jīvakasutta* (MN 55; PTS MN i 368) is a discourse in the Majjhimanikāya delivered to the Buddha's personal physician, Jīvaka Komārabhacca [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 1995]. After hearing sectarian criticisms that animals were being slaughtered specifically for the Buddha and the saṅgha, Jīvaka questions him regarding monastic regulations on meat-eating [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 1995]. The Buddha denies the charge and explains the principle of "threefold purity," permitting monks to accept meat offered on alms rounds only if they have not seen, heard, or suspected that the animal was killed deliberately for them [Keown 2005; Shulman 2014]. The discourse enumerates the demerit and evil deeds accrued by anyone who slaughters an animal for the Tathāgata or his disciples [Keown 2005], describes the meditative cultivation of the four *brahmavihāra*s (loving-kindness, compassion, altruistic joy, and equanimity) [Bodhi 1995; Analayo 2011], affirms that the Buddha has eradicated all defilements through compassion [Analayo 2011], and outlines the tranquil indifference required of a monk receiving meal invitations [Galasek 2016]. It also illustrates the high veneration lay devotees accorded to Buddhist monks over wandering ascetics of other sects [Bechert et al. 1997].
DharmaNexus records Pali-internal textual reuse across 82 texts, including large shared segments with AN 3 (§6.2–6.11), SN 42 (§2.1–3.3), AN 4 (§8–10.2–8–10.5), MN 83, and the Vinaya *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* (Kd 6), alongside cross-linguistic alignments with the Tibetan *Mahāsūtrasamuccaya* (D 3961), the Tibetan *Vinayavibhaṅga* (D 3), and the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) [DharmaNexus].
